newsitem.title: INDIA: India defers Singapore Airlines proposal.
newsitem.headline: India defers Singapore Airlines proposal.

text.p: The Indian cabinet on Tuesday deferred discussion on a controversial proposed tie-up between India's Tata group and Singapore Airlines Ltd which has split the government.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency said the issue did not come up for discussion because Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim was not in New Delhi.

The Industry Ministry last week approved the $600 million plan by Tata Industries Ltd and SIA to set up a domestic airline. "The proposal has been sent to the cabinet," a senior Industry Ministry official told Reuters earlier on Tuesday.
The Industry Ministry's recommendation flew in the face of strong opposition from Ibrahim, who wants a new aviation policy that would ban foreign investment in domestic airlines.

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs was earlier expected to discuss the proposal, which for some foreign investors has become a litmus test of the centre-left government's commitment to economic reform.
The controversial Tata-SIA tie-up was cleared in December by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board and forwarded to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet.
The board is a panel of senior government officials attached to the Industry Ministry which can approve foreign investment up to six billion rupees ($170 million).
SIA and Tata Industries submitted their proposal to launch the airline in February 1995. The Tatas planned to take a 60 percent stake, with SIA holding the rest.
Since then, the proposal has languished in the government, caught in a high-stakes battle over whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.
Ibrahim, a close ally of Deve Gowda, has been joined by communist partners in the 13-party United Front coalition in opposing the joint venture, arguing it would harm state-owned Indian Airlines.
